items.stem: Which of the following best describes "extraneous variable"?
options: A sampling technique in which participants volunteer, for example by responding to an advertisement
A sampling technique in which initial participants recruit further participants from their own networks, used for hard-to-reach groups
A statistical relationship between two co-variables, expressed by a coefficient between -1 and +1
Any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV if not controlled
items.answer: Any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV if not controlled
items.markingKey: D. "extraneous variable" is any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV if not controlled.

items.stem: Explain how the findings of Charlton et al. (2000) provide evidence about natural experiments as a way to study an IV that cannot ethically be manipulated.
items.answer: Findings: there was no significant increase in antisocial behaviour after TV arrived; most measures of behaviour stayed the same. Link: these results are evidence about natural experiments as a way to study an IV that cannot ethically be manipulated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (there was no significant increase in antisocial behaviour after TV arrived; most measures of behaviour stayed the same); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about natural experiments as a way to study an IV that cannot ethically be manipulated (not just restating them).

items.stem: Outline the findings of Godden and Baddeley (1975) and explain one conclusion about context-dependent retrieval in memory that can be drawn from them.
items.answer: Findings: recall was about 40% higher when the learning and recall environments matched than when they did not. Link: these results are evidence about context-dependent retrieval in memory.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (recall was about 40% higher when the learning and recall environments matched than when they did not); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about context-dependent retrieval in memory (not just restating them).

items.stem: Using the arrival of television on St Helena as an example, explain a natural experiment.
items.answer: Television was introduced to the island of St Helena in 1995; researchers recorded children's playground behaviour before and after. The IV (presence of TV) changed naturally, not by the researcher, so the study has high ecological validity but cannot control other changes on the island
items.markingKey: Context (Television was introduced to the island of St Helena in 1995; researchers recorded children's playground behaviour before and after.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the IV (presence of TV) changed naturally, not by the researcher, so the study has high ecological validity but cannot control other changes on the island – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a natural experiment.

items.stem: Describe the study by Godden and Baddeley (1975) and explain what it shows about context-dependent retrieval in memory.
items.answer: Godden and Baddeley (1975). Aim: to investigate whether recall is better when it takes place in the same environment as learning. Method: 18 divers learned lists of 36 words either on land or 6 m underwater and recalled them either on land or underwater, giving four conditions. Findings: recall was about 40% higher when the learning and recall environments matched than when they did not Link: context-dependent retrieval in memory.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: recall was about 40% higher when the learning and recall environments matched than when they did not); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to context-dependent retrieval in memory. A study that is described but not linked cannot score more than half marks.

items.stem: In Mexico City, students rate their mood (1-10) after 20 minutes of exercise and after 20 minutes of sitting, on two different days. Explain why this study can or cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.
items.answer: Because activity (exercise vs sitting) is manipulated by the researcher and other variables are controlled, a causal claim about its effect on self-rated mood on a 1-10 scale is possible - provided extraneous variables such as those noted are controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: whether the IV is manipulated/randomly allocated; 1 mark: role of controls/confounds; 1 mark: conclusion about causality applied to this study.

items.stem: Design an experiment to test whether background music affects the recall of words. Refer to the IV, DV, hypotheses, design, sample and controls.
items.answer: IV operationalised (lyrics vs silence); DV operationalised (words recalled out of 20 after 2 minutes); H1 and H0; design justified (independent samples with random allocation or repeated measures with counterbalancing); sample and technique; standardised instructions, same room, same time; ethics.

items.stem: Evaluate the research by Charlton et al. (2000) on television and children's behaviour on St Helena.
items.answer: Strengths: natural setting - high ecological validity; longitudinal before/after measures. Limitations: no control over other changes on the island; small, close-knit community with strong social controls - limited generalisability.
items.markingKey: Strengths: natural setting - high ecological validity; longitudinal before/after measures. items.stem: Explain why laboratory experiments may lack ecological validity.
items.answer: The artificial setting and tasks (e.g. learning word lists) differ from real life, and participants know they are being studied, so behaviour may not reflect how people act in everyday situations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The artificial setting and tasks (e.g. learning word lists) differ from real life, and participants know they are being studied, so behaviour may not reflect how people act in everyday situations. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a confounding variable and an extraneous variable.
items.answer: An extraneous variable is any uncontrolled variable that might affect the DV; it becomes a confounding variable when it varies systematically with the IV, so its effect cannot be separated from the IV's.
items.markingKey: An extraneous variable is any uncontrolled variable that might affect the DV; it becomes a confounding variable when it varies systematically with the IV, so its effect cannot be separated from the IV's. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A researcher hypothesises that sleep deprivation affects reaction time. Operationalise both the IV and the DV.
items.answer: IV: hours of sleep the night before testing, e.g. normal 8 hours vs restricted to 4 hours. DV: mean reaction time in milliseconds to press a key when a light appears, over 20 trials.
items.markingKey: IV: hours of sleep the night before testing, e.g. normal 8 hours vs restricted to 4 hours. DV: mean reaction time in milliseconds to press a key when a light appears, over 20 trials.

items.stem: Critically assess the view that laboratory experiments are the most useful method in psychology. Consider at least one methodological and one ethical or cultural issue.
items.answer: Lab experiments are the strongest method for testing causal hypotheses, but their usefulness depends on the question; triangulation with field and qualitative methods is needed.
items.markingKey: For: allow causal conclusions; high control and replicability; precise measurement. Against: low ecological validity and demand characteristics; some variables cannot be manipulated ethically; WEIRD samples limit generalisability. Supported conclusion: Lab experiments are the strongest method for testing causal hypotheses, but their usefulness depends on the question; triangulation with field and qualitative methods is needed. items.stem: Which of the following was the aim of the study by Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) on laptop versus longhand note-taking?
options: To investigate whether taking notes on a laptop or by hand affects learning from lectures
To examine the association between screen time and psychological well-being in children and adolescents
To investigate whether the meaning of a colour word interferes with naming the ink colour
To investigate whether the introduction of television increased antisocial behaviour in children
items.answer: To investigate whether taking notes on a laptop or by hand affects learning from lectures
items.markingKey: A. Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) aimed to investigate whether taking notes on a laptop or by hand affects learning from lectures.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a matched pairs design reduces participant variables.
items.answer: Each participant in one condition is paired with a similar participant (e.g. same age and IQ) in the other, so key individual differences are balanced across conditions without the order effects of repeated measures.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each participant in one condition is paired with a similar participant (e.g. same age and IQ) in the other, so key individual differences are balanced across conditions without the order effects of repeated measures. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Matched pairs designs need twice as many participants as repeated measures." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Matched pairs requires different participants in each condition (like independent samples), so it needs more participants than repeated measures, but the main issue is that matching is time-consuming and never perfect.
items.markingKey: Matched pairs requires different participants in each condition (like independent samples), so it needs more participants than repeated measures, but the main issue is that matching is time-consuming and never perfect. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A researcher wants to test whether chewing gum improves concentration. Explain which experimental design you would use and why.
items.answer: Repeated measures with counterbalancing (gum vs no gum, different but equivalent tasks) controls individual differences in concentration; or independent samples if practice effects on the task are likely - justification must be linked to the study.
items.markingKey: Repeated measures with counterbalancing (gum vs no gum, different but equivalent tasks) controls individual differences in concentration; or independent samples if practice effects on the task are likely - justification must be linked to the study.

items.stem: Using Stroop (1935) as supporting evidence, explain automatic processing of word meaning.
items.answer: Stroop (1935). Aim: to investigate whether the meaning of a colour word interferes with naming the ink colour. Method: Participants named the ink colours of colour words printed in incongruent colours (e.g. "RED" in blue ink) and of colour patches/congruent stimuli; times were compared within participants. Findings: naming the ink colour of incongruent words took significantly longer than naming colour patches (about 74% longer in one experiment) Link: automatic processing of word meaning.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for accurate description of the study (aim, method, findings: naming the ink colour of incongruent words took significantly longer than naming colour patches (about 74% longer in one experiment)); up to 2 marks for explicitly linking the findings to automatic processing of word meaning. items.stem: Explain what the study by Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) suggests about the effect of note-taking method on deeper processing.
items.answer: Findings: both groups did similarly on factual questions, but longhand note-takers did better on conceptual questions; laptop users wrote more words and more verbatim notes. Link: these results are evidence about the effect of note-taking method on deeper processing.

items.stem:
Directional hypothesis: scores on the Perceived Stress Scale (range 0-40) will be higher in the week before exams than in the week after a school holiday.

Condition A (in the week before exams): 31, 12, 10, 20, 28, 28, 13, 8
Condition B (in the week after a school holiday): 26, 36, 19, 33, 13, 28, 7, 14

Calculate the mean and sample standard deviation for each condition (to 2 decimal places). State whether the descriptive statistics are in the direction predicted by the hypothesis and compare the spread of the two conditions.
items.answer: Mean A = 18.75, SD A = 9.21; mean B = 22.00, SD B = 10.34. The means are not in the predicted direction. items.stem: Discuss the extent to which the study by Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) provides convincing evidence about the effect of note-taking method on deeper processing.
items.answer: Strengths: random allocation to conditions; measured both factual and conceptual learning. Limitations: student sample from an elite US university; short-term test; a replication by Morehead et al. (2019) found weaker effects.

items.stem: Explain how the findings of Twenge and Campbell (2018) provide evidence about the limits of correlational evidence about technology.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a correlational study and an experiment.
items.answer: An experiment manipulates an IV and measures its effect on a DV, allowing causal conclusions; a correlational study measures two co-variables as they naturally occur and only shows whether they are related.

items.stem: Chloé writes: "A negative correlation means there is no relationship." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A negative correlation is a relationship in which one variable increases as the other decreases; it can be strong (e.g. -0.9).

items.stem: Outline one way in which screen time and well-being in adolescents shows the third variable problem.
items.answer: Large surveys of US adolescents found that more hours of daily screen use were associated with slightly lower well-being. Factors such as loneliness, family conflict or poor sleep could cause both high screen use and low well-being, so screens cannot be assumed to be the cause

items.stem: Describe the study by Rahe, Mahan and Arthur (1970) and explain what it shows about the correlation between stress and health.
items.answer: Rahe, Mahan and Arthur (1970). Aim: to investigate whether life change units were related to illness. Method: About 2,500 US Navy sailors on three cruisers completed the Schedule of Recent Experiences for the previous six months before a tour of duty; illness records were kept during the 6-8 month tour. Findings: there was a weak positive correlation (about +0.118) between life change units and illness scores Link: the correlation between stress and health.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "opportunity sampling".
items.answer: A sampling technique that uses people who are available and willing at the time of the study

items.stem: Explain why purposive sampling is often used in qualitative research.
items.answer: Qualitative research seeks rich, in-depth data on a specific experience, so participants are chosen because they have that experience (e.g. survivors of an earthquake); representativeness is less important than relevance.

items.stem: Sana writes: "A random sample is always representative of the target population." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Random sampling reduces bias but a small random sample can still be unrepresentative by chance; larger samples and stratification help.

items.stem: Describe the study by Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010) and explain what it shows about the problem of sampling bias in psychology.
items.answer: Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010). Aim: to review whether findings based on Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic samples can be generalised to humans in general. items.stem: Explain why opportunity samples may lead to biased findings.
items.answer: The researcher selects whoever is available (often students in one place), so the sample may share age, education and culture and differ systematically from the target population, limiting generalisability.

items.answer: Neither variable is manipulated, so a third variable may cause both (e.g. poverty causing both stress and illness), and the direction of influence is unclear (bidirectional ambiguity).

items.stem: Explain the difference between opportunity sampling and random sampling.
items.answer: Random sampling gives every member of the target population an equal chance of selection (less bias but needs a full list and is time-consuming); opportunity sampling uses whoever is available (quick and cheap but likely to be unrepresentative).

items.stem: Describe the study by Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) and explain what it shows about the effect of note-taking method on deeper processing.
items.answer: Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014). Aim: to investigate whether taking notes on a laptop or by hand affects learning from lectures. Method: Princeton students were randomly assigned to take notes on a laptop or by hand while watching TED talks, then answered factual and conceptual questions. Findings: both groups did similarly on factual questions, but longhand note-takers did better on conceptual questions; laptop users wrote more words and more verbatim notes Link: the effect of note-taking method on deeper processing.

items.stem: A school counsellor in Geneva finds r = -0.62 between hours of part-time work and exam grades. Write a suitable correlational hypothesis and explain one conclusion and one limitation.
items.answer: H1: there will be a negative correlation between weekly hours of part-time work and exam grades. items.stem: With reference to Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010), explain how research has investigated the problem of sampling bias in psychology.
items.answer: Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010). Aim: to review whether findings based on Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic samples can be generalised to humans in general. items.stem: Evaluate the research by Godden and Baddeley (1975) on context-dependent memory in divers.
items.answer: Strengths: realistic natural environments for divers; four-condition design isolates the effect of matching context. Limitations: small, specialised sample (divers); difficult to control conditions underwater (e.g. cheating, equipment problems); repeated measures may cause order effects.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an extraneous variable and a confounding variable.
items.answer: An extraneous variable is any uncontrolled variable that might affect the DV; it becomes a confounding variable when it varies systematically with the IV, so its effect cannot be separated from the IV's.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a repeated measures design and an independent samples design.
items.answer: In repeated measures the same participants do all conditions (controls participant variables but risks order effects); in independent samples different participants do each condition (no order effects but participant variables may differ).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Laboratory experiments are the most useful method in psychology."
items.answer: Lab experiments are the strongest method for testing causal hypotheses, but their usefulness depends on the question; triangulation with field and qualitative methods is needed.
